teaser: Its own painter filed it under failures. He never knew what it would become.

lesson.text: In the fall of 1889, Vincent van Gogh wrote to a painter friend about some recent canvases with stars that were, he admitted, too big. He called the attempt a failure and said he had had enough of that sort of thing. His brother Theo, an art dealer and his most loyal supporter, was not convinced by the picture either. The picture was this one.

He painted it in June, a month after checking himself into the asylum of Saint-Paul-de-Mausole, near Saint-Rémy in the south of France. Months earlier, in Arles, a breakdown had ended with him cutting off part of his own ear. At the asylum he had a bedroom with a barred window facing east, and a second empty room on the ground floor to use as a studio.

Van Gogh was not allowed to paint in his bedroom. So this night sky was painted in daylight, downstairs, from memory and from sketches. The window view he knew by heart: he painted it more than twenty times, at every hour and in every weather.

Around the start of June he told Theo that he had looked out long before sunrise and seen nothing but the morning star, which looked very big. The morning star is not a star at all. It is the planet Venus, and it really was shining in the dawn sky over Provence that spring.
Eleven stars burn in this sky. One is whiter and larger than the rest: Venus. Which one?

spots.title: The morning star
spots.text: Just right of the cypress, low in the sky. Its core is yellow, but the halo is painted in rings of white and pale green, short dashes circling like ripples around a dropped stone.

lesson.text: Those rings of dashes are the real subject here. Van Gogh loads his brush with thick paint and lays it down in strokes you can count, each one aimed in a direction. Thick, raised paint like this is called impasto. In most older painting the brush hides itself. Here it tells you how fast the hand moved and where it was going.

lesson.title: A sky in motion
lesson.text: Follow the paint from right to left and watch what the strokes do.

spots.title: Moon or sun?
spots.text: An orange crescent sits inside a yellow disc of light, itself ringed with pale green. The glow is so strong that the moon almost reads as a sun.

spots.title: The great spiral
spots.text: Two currents of blue and white curl into each other like waves. Nothing in a real sky looks like this. It is the picture's invented heart, and the reason Theo hesitated.

spots.title: A band of light
spots.text: Above the hills runs a pale, milky stream of strokes. It may be the first light of dawn or a bank of mist. Either way, it flows in the same direction as the spiral.

lesson.text: So the sky is half observed and half made up. That was a deliberate, risky choice. His friends Paul Gauguin and Émile Bernard urged him to paint from imagination instead of copying nature. Vincent usually resisted: he needed something real in front of him. This canvas is one of the few times he gave in, which is exactly why he later doubted it.

Astronomers have checked the sky of mid-June 1889. Venus was indeed bright before dawn, but the moon was not a thin crescent that week. It was closer to three-quarters full. Van Gogh chose the shape he wanted.

Now the lower half. From his window he could see a wheat field, a wall and the low Alpilles hills. He could not see a village. The houses and the church come from elsewhere, and the big dark shape in front was not in his view either. He added it all to give the swirling sky something to push against.
Two verticals answer the rolling sky, and one long line ties the picture together.

lines.label: The cypress
lines.text: A dark flame climbing from the bottom edge almost to the top. It is the only thing that joins earth and sky, and its twisting strokes echo the spiral above.

lines.label: The steeple
lines.text: A thin spire, tiny beside the tree, repeats the same upward gesture. Human building looks fragile next to what grows and what burns overhead.

lines.label: The hills
lines.text: The Alpilles rise from left to right in blue waves, outlined in dark paint. They carry the sky's movement down toward the sleeping houses.

lesson.text: Cypresses fascinated him that summer. He wrote that they were as beautiful in line and proportion as an Egyptian obelisk, and wondered why nobody had painted them the way he saw them. In Mediterranean countries they are also the trees of cemeteries. Many viewers read that into the picture. He never said so himself.
The pointed spire looks more like the churches of the Netherlands, where Vincent grew up, than the stubbier bell tower of Saint-Rémy. A homesick northern steeple has slipped into a Provençal night.
This is not a view through a window. It is a real dawn sky, a remembered village and an invented whirlwind, joined by one rhythm of brushstrokes.

Vincent died in July 1890, thirteen months after painting it. The canvas stayed in the family, cared for by Theo's widow Johanna, who spent decades making her brother-in-law known. It passed through several owners before the Museum of Modern Art in New York acquired it in 1941.

spots.title: Lit windows
spots.text: Small squares of orange and yellow in the dark blue houses. A few people are awake. Their lamps use the same colors as the stars, as if the two were related.

spots.title: The church
spots.text: Its own windows stay dark. The outlines are drawn with firm dark strokes, a habit Van Gogh took from the Japanese prints he collected.

spots.title: Inside the cypress
spots.text: Not black: dark green, brown and deep blue, in long curling strokes. The tree is painted with the same wavy motion as the sky, only darker.

spots.title: A star's halo
spots.text: An orange center, then a ring of yellow, then one of pale green dashes. Every star gets its own little whirl.

spots.title: Olive groves
spots.text: The round tufts of trees are curled like the clouds. From the fields to the stars, the whole world is drawn with one handwriting.

spots.title: Bare canvas
spots.text: Along the left edge the paint stops short and the pale weave shows through. He worked fast and did not go back to tidy the border.

lesson.text: Go back to that letter about stars that were too big. What he judged a mistake is what millions now come to see: a sky that looks the way a night can feel. The painter was a poor judge of his own picture, and that may be a comfort the next time you dismiss something you made.

quiz.question: How did Van Gogh himself judge this kind of star painting a few months later?
options: As the best thing he had done
As a simple copy of nature
quiz.explanation: He wrote to a friend that the stars were too big and called the attempt a failure.

quiz.question: When was the night sky actually painted?
options: At night, from his bedroom window
In daylight, in a ground-floor studio
quiz.explanation: He was not allowed to paint in his bedroom, so he worked by day from memory and sketches.

quiz.question: What is the large white “star” just right of the cypress?
quiz.explanation: Venus, the morning star, was bright before dawn that spring, and he mentioned it in a letter.

quiz.question: Which part of the scene could Van Gogh NOT see from his window?
quiz.explanation: The village and the steeple were added from memory and imagination.

quiz.question: What does “impasto” mean?
options: Paint thinned until it is transparent
Thick paint that stands up from the canvas
quiz.explanation: Impasto is thick, raised paint in which each brushstroke stays visible.

quiz.question: Which museum acquired the painting in 1941?
options: The Museum of Modern Art, New York

facts.text: The moon was really a thin crescent on the nights before Van Gogh painted the picture.
facts.explanation: Astronomers found it was closer to three-quarters full; he chose the crescent shape.

facts.text: Van Gogh painted the view from his asylum window more than twenty times.
facts.explanation: He returned to that eastern view at every hour and in every weather.

facts.text: The cypress in the foreground is painted in pure black.
facts.explanation: It is built from dark green, brown and deep blue strokes.
